title: A Religious Leader Asked Jesus, “Who Is My Neighbor?” Jesus Answered With a Story That Made the Wrong Person the Hero.
paragraphs: A Religious Leader Asked Jesus, “Who Is My Neighbor?” Jesus Answered With a Story That Made the Wrong Person the Hero.

The Good Samaritan is not merely a lesson about being nice to strangers. It is a confrontation with the human heart—a story about the people we excuse ourselves from loving, the mercy we cannot earn, and the Savior who refuses to let religion become a hiding place.
There is something dangerous about asking Jesus a question when you have already decided what answer you want.
Because Jesus has a way of answering the question beneath the question.

And sometimes His answer dismantles the little courtroom we have built inside ourselves—the courtroom where we are always innocent, our enemies are always guilty, our compassion always has reasonable limits, and God conveniently agrees with us.
That is what happened on a road in Luke 10.
A man stood up.
Not an atheist.
Not a pagan.
Not someone ignorant of Scripture.
Luke calls him a νομικός — nomikos, a lawyer, meaning an expert in the Law of Moses.
He knew the commandments.
He knew the theological vocabulary.
He knew how religious discussions worked.
And he asked Jesus one of the greatest questions a human being could possibly ask:

“Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
—Luke 10:25
But Luke tells us something important about the question.
The man stood up ἐκπειράζων αὐτόν — ekpeirazōn auton.
He was “testing Him.”
This was not simply a desperate sinner crying, “How can I be saved?”
There was a test inside the question.
Jesus responded by directing the expert back to the very Law he claimed to understand.

“What is written in the law? how readest thou?”
—Luke 10:26, KJV
The man answered beautifully.
Love God completely.
Love your neighbor as yourself.
He was drawing from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18.
And Jesus said:

“Thou hast answered right: this do, and thou shalt live.”
—Luke 10:28, KJV
That should have ended the conversation.
It didn’t.
Because knowing the commandment and surrendering to the commandment are two very different things.
Luke then gives us one devastating sentence:

“But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour?”
—Luke 10:29, KJV
There it is.
Willing to justify himself.
The Greek is even more revealing:
ὁ δὲ θέλων δικαιῶσαι ἑαυτόν — ho de thelōn dikaiōsai heauton
Literally, he was wanting to justify himself.
That sentence is the doorway into the entire parable.
The man did not merely need information about neighbors.
He needed a boundary.
He needed to know where his obligation ended.
How far does love have to go?
Who qualifies?
Who doesn’t?
Who can I walk past without violating the commandment?
Who is close enough to deserve my compassion?
And, perhaps more uncomfortably:
Who am I biblically permitted not to love?
We still ask that question.
We just dress it differently.
“Lord, surely You don't mean him.”
“Surely You don't expect me to forgive her.”
“You know what they did.”
“You know what they said about me.”
“You know how many times I helped them.”
“You know what kind of people they are.”
“They chose this.”
“They hurt me first.”
“They believe differently.”
“They vote differently.”
“They worship differently.”
“They betrayed me.”
“They embarrassed me.”
“They never apologized.”
“Surely, Jesus… there has to be a line.”
And Jesus begins telling a story.
“A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho…”
No name.
No résumé.
No ethnicity explicitly identified.
No explanation of whether he deserved help.
Just a man.
Traveling.
And then everything collapsed.
He fell among robbers.
They stripped him.
Beat him.
Took what he had.
And left him.
Luke's description is chilling:
ἡμιθανῆ — hēmithanē
“Half-dead.”
Try not to read that too quickly.
Picture him.
Dust sticking to blood.
Clothing torn away.
Possessions gone.
Body broken.
Breathing, perhaps, but barely.
Unable to rescue himself.
Unable to negotiate.
Unable to prove that he was worthy of assistance.
Unable to offer repayment.
All he could do was lie there.
And then footsteps came.
A priest.
Of all people.
If anyone should understand mercy, surely the priest should.
Jesus says:

“And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side.”
—Luke 10:31, KJV
He saw him.
That matters.
This was not ignorance.
The wounded man was not invisible.
He was seen.
And passed.
Then another man approached.
A Levite.
Another person associated with Israel's religious life.
Perhaps this time.
Perhaps he will stop.
Luke says he came to the place.
He saw the man.
And he also passed by on the other side.
Two religious men.
Two sets of eyes.
Two opportunities for mercy.
Two decisions to keep moving.
Jesus does not tell us their motives.
That matters too.
We should resist inventing excuses the text itself does not give them.
Maybe they were afraid.
Maybe they were hurried.
Maybe they suspected danger.
Maybe they had explanations that sounded perfectly reasonable inside their own minds.
Jesus does not tell us.
He tells us what they did.
They saw suffering.
And they passed by.
That should disturb every Christian who has ever learned how to explain why somebody else's pain is not our responsibility.
Because you can know Scripture and still cross the road.
You can attend worship and still cross the road.
You can post Bible verses and still cross the road.
You can defend Christian doctrine online and still cross the road.
You can sing about the love of God while carefully avoiding the person whose suffering would inconvenience your schedule.
You can be religiously correct and mercifully absent.
Then Jesus introduces the third traveler.
And this is where the story becomes scandalous.
“But a certain Samaritan…”
Stop there.
A Samaritan.
Jesus did not choose the hero His audience might naturally expect.

The Gospels themselves preserve evidence of the social and religious hostility between Jews and Samaritans. In John 4:9, the Samaritan woman is astonished that Jesus, a Jew, asks her for a drink, and the text explicitly notes the strained relations between Jews and Samaritans. In Luke 9:52–53, a Samaritan village refuses to receive Jesus because He is traveling toward Jerusalem.
So when Jesus said:
Σαμαρίτης δέ τις — Samaritēs de tis
“But a certain Samaritan…”
the story had crossed an uncomfortable line.
The person expected to be outside the moral circle was walking into the center of the story.
The outsider was about to do what the religious insiders had failed to do.
And then comes one of the most beautiful words in the passage.
The Samaritan saw the wounded man and:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη — esplagchnisthē
“He was moved with compassion.”
This is not detached sympathy.
The verb describes deep, inward compassion—a visceral movement of mercy.
He saw him…
and something moved inside him.
Then compassion became action.
He approached.
He bound the wounds.
He poured on oil and wine.
He lifted the wounded man onto his own animal.
He brought him to an inn.
He cared for him.
The next day, he gave the innkeeper two denarii and promised to cover additional legitimate expense when he returned.
Notice what mercy cost him.
Time.
Resources.
Comfort.
Convenience.
Money.
Attention.
Risk.
Interruption.
Mercy was not something he felt while continuing down the road.
Mercy changed his itinerary.
And suddenly the question asked at the beginning of the story starts collapsing.
“Who is my neighbor?”
The lawyer wanted Jesus to identify the proper recipient of neighbor-love.
Jesus instead told him about a man who became a neighbor through mercy.
Then Jesus turned the question around:

“Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?”
—Luke 10:36, KJV
Look carefully at what Jesus did.
The original question was essentially:
Who qualifies as my neighbor?
Jesus' closing question becomes:
Which man acted as a neighbor?
The lawyer answered:

“He that shewed mercy on him.”
—Luke 10:37, KJV
Even that response is striking.
He does not say, “The Samaritan.”
He says:
“The one who showed mercy.”
And Jesus answered:
“Go, and do thou likewise.”
That is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because Jesus does not allow us to admire the Samaritan from a safe distance.
He sends us toward the road.
Toward wounded people.
Toward inconvenient people.
Toward people who cannot repay us.
And sometimes toward people we would never have chosen.
The parable exposes something ugly in us.
We love asking who deserves mercy because that allows us to remain the judge.
Jesus asks whether we are willing to become merciful.
We ask:
“Who is worthy of my love?”
Jesus moves us toward another question:
“Will you love the person God has placed in front of you?”
And this reaches far beyond giving money to someone in need.
Maybe the person lying beside your emotional road is your spouse.
Maybe you have been living in the same house while walking past each other's wounds.
Maybe it is your child.
Your father.
Your mother.
Your brother.
Your sister.
Someone at church.
Someone who disappointed you.
Someone everybody else quietly abandoned.
Maybe it is the person whose name makes your chest tighten.
The person you blocked.
The person you avoid.
The person you privately decided no longer deserves kindness.
This does not mean Scripture commands you to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Biblical love does not require pretending evil is good, eliminating wise boundaries, enabling sin, or refusing appropriate protection and justice.
Mercy is not the denial of truth.
Jesus is full of grace and truth.
But neither can “boundaries” become a holy-sounding word we use to baptize hatred.
There is a difference between protecting yourself from ongoing harm and feeding bitterness until another person's suffering no longer matters to you.
Jesus knows the difference.
And so does the heart when the Holy Spirit begins searching it.
Maybe the most frightening possibility is this:
You can spend years trying not to become the wounded man…
and slowly become the person who walks past him.
You survive your own pain.
You build walls.
You become careful.
Suspicious.
Harder.
You tell yourself that nobody helped you, so why should you help them?
And without realizing it, yesterday's wounded traveler becomes tomorrow's passerby.
But Jesus interrupts that cycle.
Because the Gospel does something human resentment cannot do.
The Gospel reminds us that before we start congratulating ourselves for being the Samaritan, we should remember how desperately we needed mercy.
We were not saved because we had accumulated enough moral points.
We did not negotiate our way into grace.
We could not cleanse our own guilt.
Sin was not a shallow scratch requiring motivational advice.
Scripture says:

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
And:

“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
That changes everything.
The deepest Christian motivation for mercy is not:
“Be nicer so God will finally love you.”
It is:
In Christ, look at the mercy God has shown sinners who could never purchase it.
Jesus Christ went to the cross.
Our sin was real.
God's holiness was real.
Judgment was real.
And the Son of God willingly gave Himself.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ, not because sin does not matter, but because Jesus dealt with sin at a cost we could never pay.
The Gospel does not merely tell wounded sinners to crawl harder.
It announces a Savior.
And when grace reaches a human heart, it begins changing how that heart sees everybody else.
You cannot earn salvation by becoming a Good Samaritan.
That would reverse the Gospel.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith, not the product of our works or moral heroism (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But do not stop reading at verse 9.
Ephesians 2:10 says believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
Grace saves us.
Then grace transforms us.
We do not show mercy in order to purchase Christ.
We show mercy because Christ has taken hold of us.
That distinction matters.
Christian compassion is not the admission price into heaven.
It is one of the fruits that should increasingly appear in a life being transformed by the King of heaven.
So perhaps the Good Samaritan is asking you something tonight.
Not merely:
“Do you understand this parable?”
But:
Who have you been walking past?
Whose pain did you notice but decide was too inconvenient?
Whose name have you turned into a category instead of remembering they are a human being made in God's image?
Who became “those people” to you?
Who have you reduced to their worst moment?
And what if the person Jesus is commanding you to treat as a neighbor is the person you hoped He would exclude?
Be honest.
This may hit harder than you expected.
Maybe there is another side too.
Maybe right now you are not identifying with the priest.
Or the Levite.
Or even the Samaritan.
Maybe you feel like the man in the dirt.
Half-alive.
Stripped by betrayal.
Beaten down by consequences.
Robbed by addiction.
Crushed by grief.
Exhausted from fighting battles nobody knows exist.
People have looked at you and kept walking.
Even religious people.
Perhaps especially religious people.
And somewhere inside you, you began wondering whether God would walk past too.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Jesus is not ashamed of ruined people who come to Him.
He touched lepers.
He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He received the rejected.
He restored failures.
He forgave the repentant.
He welcomed the broken.
He went to a cross between criminals.
Peter denied Him—and Peter's story was not over.
A thief dying beside Him turned toward Him—and his story was not over.
Saul persecuted the church—and his story was not over.
Scandal did not get the final sentence.
Grace did.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives and then says, “Follow Me.”
Grace that finds sinners but refuses to leave them unchanged.
Grace that produces repentance.
Grace that destroys our excuses.
Grace that teaches enemies to become neighbors.
Grace that turns wounded people into people who bind wounds.
Grace that takes a heart filled with hatred and teaches it to kneel before Jesus.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe today your next act of obedience is not dramatic.
Maybe it is a phone call.
An apology.
A meal.
A hospital visit.
A private gift.
A prayer.
A conversation.
A decision to stop humiliating somebody whose sin became public.
A decision to forgive while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
A decision to see a human being where you previously saw only an enemy.
Maybe your Jericho road is not somewhere far away.
Maybe it is your Facebook feed.
Your workplace.
Your church.
Your dining table.
Your family group chat.
Your neighborhood.
Maybe someone is bleeding where everybody can see them…
and everybody keeps scrolling.
Do not merely “like” a story about mercy.
Become a neighbor.
And if this article exposed someone you have been walking past, do not rush away from that conviction.
Take it to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask Him to remove bitterness.
Ask Him for wisdom where reconciliation is complicated.
Ask Him for courage where mercy will cost something.
Ask Him to make your life look increasingly like a life that has actually encountered grace.
Then make the comment section more than an algorithm.
Make it an altar of honesty.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your story.
But sometimes three honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer:
I am not the only one still fighting.

Not because saving a post is spiritual obedience by itself, but because there may come a day when resentment feels justified again, when somebody wounds you again, when compassion becomes expensive again, and you need to remember the road between Jerusalem and Jericho.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Send it privately to the friend whose faith is exhausted.
Send it to the Christian who has become discouraged by hypocrisy.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about religious people proving they are better than everyone else.
Let them encounter Jesus instead.
And if Gospel Warrior is helping you encounter Scripture, conviction, grace, healing, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ more deeply, stay close.
We will never place a price tag on grace.
But generosity can be an act through which believers intentionally help Gospel-centered work reach farther.

Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, encouraging wounded believers, confronting comfortable religion, calling sinners toward repentance, and pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
The Samaritan's road is still in front of us.
People are still wounded.
Religion can still become an excuse.
Enemies can still become neighbors.
And Jesus is still asking what we will do with the mercy we ourselves have received.
One day nobody will remember how polished our Christian image looked.
But heaven sees the cup of cold water.
The unseen generosity.
The forgiveness that cost us tears.
The wounded person we refused to abandon.
The enemy we stopped dehumanizing.
The stranger we finally saw.
The sinner we loved enough to tell the truth to.
The broken believer we helped carry when they could no longer carry themselves.
And above all, the Savior whose mercy made any of our mercy possible.
So go back to the road.
Look again.
The person you were prepared to walk past may be the very place where Christ is exposing what your religion has done to your heart.
And perhaps the greatest scandal in the story was never that the Samaritan became the hero.
Perhaps the scandal is that sinners like us received mercy from God—and then somehow imagined we could afford to become stingy with it.
Never forget this: the road where somebody else's wounds interrupt your plans may become the road where Jesus reveals what grace has actually done to your heart.
